findings.body: Interpolating `owner_id` directly into SQL is a security-sensitive addition unrelated to the stated refactor. Use the cursor's parameter-binding mechanism rather than constructing the query with an f-string.
findings.failure_scenario: If an owner ID contains a quote or attacker-controlled SQL, the resulting query can read other customers' orders or execute unintended SQL.

findings.body: The default `events` list is created once and mutated on every call that omits the argument. Later callers receive event types recorded by earlier callers. Use `None` as the default and create a fresh list inside the function.
findings.failure_scenario: One caller records a shipment event without passing a list; a later caller does the same and receives the earlier caller's event type in the returned list.
findings.title: Prevent cross-request event leakage from the shared default list

findings.body: Membership checks against the growing `seen` list make deduplication quadratic for distinct labels. Track membership in a set while retaining the `labels` list for first-seen order.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller supplies a large number of distinct payment labels, causing each successive lookup to scan more labels and potentially tying up a worker.
findings.title: Avoid quadratic work when deduplicating payment labels

findings.body: The nested loops do work proportional to `len(carriers) * len(zones) * len(weights)`, although every carrier receives the same count. Count nonempty zones and positive weights once, then assign their product to each carrier.
findings.failure_scenario: Large carrier, zone, and weight lists cause the function to execute an enormous number of iterations, exhausting request CPU time.
findings.title: Bound tariff-route work instead of iterating every combination

findings.body: The function documents that records arrive in chronological order, so sorting allocates and processes the entire input unnecessarily. Read the last record directly, preserving constant-time behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A large queue-record list makes a newest-ID lookup allocate a sorted copy and consume substantial CPU and memory instead of reading one element.
findings.title: Avoid sorting the entire queue to read its newest ID

findings.body: Starting the range at 1 skips entries[0] on every call, so the returned ranking is incomplete.
findings.failure_scenario: When a single invoice entry is provided, the function returns an empty list instead of that entry; with multiple entries, it always drops the first.
findings.title: Include the first invoice entry in the ranking

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and produces a naive timestamp. The resulting created_at string has no UTC offset, so consumers cannot reliably distinguish it from local time.
findings.failure_scenario: When a consumer parses created_at and compares it with a timezone-aware datetime, the comparison raises TypeError.
findings.title: Use a timezone-aware UTC timestamp

findings.body: The condition uses a fixed 5000 instead of the threshold argument, so callers cannot control which rows are flagged.
findings.failure_scenario: When threshold is 1000 and a row's total is 2000, the function omits the row even though it crosses the requested review threshold.

findings.title: Make the queued-order docstring match the query

findings.body: The docstring says the function ranks invoice entries, but the loop starts at position 1 and omits the first entry. Include it in the ranking, or explicitly document why it is excluded.
findings.title: Account for the first entry in the ranking contract

findings.title: Clarify what shipment events the result contains
